regular_trained_start.label: Army trade-trained strength
regular_trained_start.description: Army Full Time Trade Trained Strength (FTTTS): UK Regulars and Gurkhas who have completed Phase 2 training.
regular_trained_start.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 3a

regular_untrained_start.label: Army untrained strength
regular_untrained_start.description: Army Full-Time Untrained Personnel (UK Regulars and Gurkhas) in Phase 1 or Phase 2 training.
regular_untrained_start.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 3e

regular_gains_annual.label: Baseline training output
regular_gains_annual.description: Army Gains to Trade Trained Strength in the 12 months to 30 June 2026. Used as the baseline annual throughput of the Army training pipeline.
regular_gains_annual.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 5b

regular_untrained_intake_annual.label: Regular untrained intake
regular_untrained_intake_annual.description: Untrained intake to the Army in the 12 months to 30 June 2026. Regular recruiting continues during the game and occupies baseline training capacity.
regular_untrained_intake_annual.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 5a

regular_voluntary_outflow_annual.label: Trade-trained voluntary outflow
regular_voluntary_outflow_annual.description: Army trade-trained voluntary outflow in the 12 months to 30 June 2026. Removed by stop-loss. Other outflow (time expiry, medical, death) is not modelled.
regular_voluntary_outflow_annual.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Tables 4 and 5d

regular_outflow_intent_pct.label: Army intending to leave early
regular_outflow_intent_pct.description: Share of the Army answering that they plan to leave before the end of their engagement, to leave as soon as they can, or that they have already put in their notice.
regular_outflow_intent_pct.source: MoD, UK Regular Armed Forces Continuous Attitude Survey Results 2026, published 28 May 2026, Annex B Table B12.1 (question A173), Army
regular_outflow_intent_pct.note: 10% leave before the end of the current engagement + 6% as soon as I can + 3% notice already in, against 42% staying as long as they can and 22% to the end of the engagement (n = 2,446). The same total has run 17-23 every year since 2019, so 19 is a settled level rather than a reading of the crisis.

regular_outflow_intent_conversion.label: Intention converted to departure each year
regular_outflow_intent_conversion.description: Share of those intending to leave early who actually leave within the year. The gap between what people say and what they do.
regular_outflow_intent_conversion.source: Derived from MoD, UK Regular Armed Forces Continuous Attitude Survey Results 2026, published 28 May 2026, Annex B Table B12.1 (question A173), Army; MoD Service Personnel Statistics, 1 July 2026, Tables 4 and 5d
regular_outflow_intent_conversion.derivation: Realised outflow over trade-trained strength = 3,311 / 70,951 = 4.6666% a year. Intention to leave early = 19%. 4.6666 / 19 = 0.2456. Carried to four places because the split has to reconstruct the published annual figure: 70,951 x 19% x 0.2456 = 3,310.9 against the 3,311 the Army reports.
regular_outflow_intent_conversion.note: Holding this constant and letting intention move is the model's claim about what a minister can change: they cannot make people who want to leave stay, but what they do to Service life moves how many want to.

outflow_intent_max_pct.label: Ceiling on intention to leave
outflow_intent_max_pct.description: Highest the intention-to-leave figure may be driven by events and by stop-loss.
outflow_intent_max_pct.rationale: AFCAS has never recorded the Army outside 17-23 in twenty years of the series, so any figure here is an extrapolation beyond the evidence. 40 is a little over twice the baseline: bad enough to be a crisis, short of claiming the Army would dissolve. Nothing in the deck can reach it on its own; it is a guard against compounding.

stop_loss_leak_fraction.label: Outflow that stop-loss cannot stop
stop_loss_leak_fraction.description: Share of voluntary outflow that continues even with engagements compulsorily extended.
stop_loss_leak_fraction.rationale: Compulsion does not reach medical discharge, discharge on disciplinary grounds, or a commission the Crown declines to extend, and AFCAS puts intention at 19% against 4.67% realised, so what stop-loss dams does not go away. A quarter is an assumption; the direction is not.

stop_loss_intent_add_monthly.label: Intention added each month under stop-loss
stop_loss_intent_add_monthly.description: Points added to the intention-to-leave figure for every month engagements are held open compulsorily.
stop_loss_intent_add_monthly.rationale: Of those who have put their notice in, 50% cite the impact of Service life on family and personal life, the most cited reason by some way (AFCAS 2026, Table FP.1). Being held past the end of an engagement is that factor exactly. Half a point a month is +6 over a division and +10 over a corps: enough to be felt late, not enough to decide the game.

training_attrition.label: Training attrition
training_attrition.description: Share of untrained entrants who leave before completing Phase 2. Derived as Army untrained outflow (2,022) divided by Army untrained intake (7,771) in the 12 months to 30 June 2026.
training_attrition.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Tables 5a and 5c

regular_deployable_fraction.label: Deployable regular slice
regular_deployable_fraction.description: Share of the trade-trained regular Army that can be committed to the new formation without breaking existing commitments (Estonia, Cyprus, Falklands, UK resilience, the training estate, the readiness cycle and the medically non-deployable).
regular_deployable_fraction.rationale: The premise is that the division must be raised on top of the standing Army's current tasks: overseas commitments, the readiness cycle, the training organisation and the medically non-deployable leave only a thin uncommitted slice. The whole regular Army counts in the ledger but only this slice counts toward Force Ready.

junior_leaders.label: Junior leaders
junior_leaders.description: Army junior leadership cadre: Corporals (OR-4), Sergeants (OR-6), Staff Sergeants (OR-7), Second Lieutenants and Lieutenants (OF-1) and Captains (OF-2).
junior_leaders.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 11a (rank structure at 1 April 2026)

junior_leader_ratio.label: Soldiers per junior leader
junior_leader_ratio.description: Soldiers the Army mans itself at per junior leader: its trade-trained strength divided by its Corporal-to-Captain cadre. Applied to everyone raised on top of the standing Army who does not arrive as a formed unit.
junior_leader_ratio.source: Derived from MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Tables 3a and 11a
junior_leader_ratio.derivation: Trade-trained strength over the junior-leader cadre = 70,951 / 29,563 = 2.4
junior_leader_ratio.note: This is the whole-Army manning ratio, staff and headquarters posts included, not a doctrinal section-commander ratio. It is used because it is the rate at which the Army actually finds leaders for the soldiers it has. The instructor ratio is a separate parameter (instructor_ratio).

instructor_ratio.label: Recruits per instructor
instructor_ratio.description: Recruits one junior leader can instruct in the training estate. Sets how many junior leaders each training-capacity purchase takes out of the field force.
instructor_ratio.rationale: Infantry section of eight soldiers under a corporal; Phase 1 training-platoon instructor ratios are similar.

promotion_course_months.label: Junior-leader cadre course
promotion_course_months.description: Months a cadre course takes to turn a trade-trained soldier into a junior leader.
promotion_course_months.source: Maroni TD, Myers SD, Draper J, Ashdown KM, Walker FS, Alexander B, Blacker SD (2025), 'An ergonomic assessment of British Army Infantry career training courses to identify opportunities for evidence-based interventions to enhance role-related physical fitness', Ergonomics 69(2), pp. 206-220
promotion_course_months.derivation: The paper's abstract states it assessed 'the British Army's 8-week Platoon Sergeant and Section Commander Battle Courses (PSBC, SCBC)'. Converted with the same weeks-to-months rounding the conscript course uses (section 5): round(8 x 12 / 52) = 2.
promotion_course_months.note: The Section Commanders' Battle Course is the qualifying course for substantive Corporal in the infantry. The figure is taken from a peer-reviewed study whose subjects were soldiers on those courses, so the duration is a fact about its own method rather than a claim repeated at second hand; two of its seven authors are listed with Army Headquarters (Personnel Policy) affiliations. The MoD's own Infantry Battle School page states no duration and refuses automated fetching. Beware the widely quoted 16 weeks: that is the Platoon Commanders' Battle Course, which is an officer course and a different thing.

promotion_cadre_size.label: Junior leaders per cadre course
promotion_cadre_size.description: Trade-trained soldiers promoted to junior leader by one accelerated cadre course.
promotion_cadre_size.source: Derived from MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics, Tables 3a and 11a (trained strength and junior-leader strength) and the Army's annual trained output
promotion_cadre_size.derivation: One course pulls forward about one month of the Army's own promotion output. Junior leaders are 29,563 of the 70,951 trade-trained, 41.67%; in a steady state the cadre holds its share, so the flow into it is 41.67% of the 5,933 a year the pipeline graduates = 2,472 a year, or 206 a month.
promotion_cadre_size.note: The quarterly statistics publish strength, intake and outflow by rank but not promotion flows, so there is no published count of promotions to Corporal to read directly; this reconstructs the steady-state flow from three figures that are published. It is the rate, not a capacity: the Infantry Battle School's throughput is not modelled, and a minister can run courses back to back for as long as the cadre can staff them.

eff_promoted_leader.label: Effectiveness of an accelerated junior leader
eff_promoted_leader.description: What a junior leader promoted early is worth against one who reached the rank in the normal course of a career.
eff_promoted_leader.rationale: The one frank assumption in this mechanic, in the way the refusal conversion is in the refusal model: no figure for the effectiveness of accelerated promotion exists or is likely to. What is being discounted is narrow, which argues for a high value rather than a low one - the soldier has passed the same 8-week course as anyone else, and what they lack is the years in rank behind it, not the training. Set level with the recalled ex-regular's 0.6, which discounts them by the same order for the mirror-image problem: the ex-regular had the experience and lost it, the accelerated corporal has the course and has not yet earned it. The range runs from a third, at which the promotion is a fiction, to four fifths, at which time in rank hardly matters and the Army would have no reason not to promote everyone early.
eff_promoted_leader.note: Historically this is war-substantive and acting rank, which is how every mass mobilisation has answered the same problem. The model simplifies in one direction and it is worth stating: a promoted soldier stops doing the trade they were trained for, and that loss is not charged - the costs modelled are the political capital, the action slot, the cadre held back to instruct, and this discount.

junior_leaders_spareable_fraction.label: Spareable junior leaders
junior_leaders_spareable_fraction.description: Share of the junior leadership cadre that can be taken out of regular units to instruct or lead new formations before regular units stop functioning.
junior_leaders_spareable_fraction.rationale: Regular battalions need most of their own corporals and sergeants. Stripping more than roughly a third hollows out the units that are supposed to be the core of the force; Russia's 2022 mobilisation showed what happens when mobilised men arrive without leaders.

leaders_per_capacity_purchase.label: Instructors per capacity purchase
leaders_per_capacity_purchase.description: Junior leaders diverted from the field force for each +5,000/yr block of training capacity.
leaders_per_capacity_purchase.source: Derived from the capacity bought per purchase and the instructor ratio
leaders_per_capacity_purchase.derivation: Capacity bought per purchase over the instructor ratio = 5,000 / 8 = 625

reserve_volunteer_trained.label: Army Reserve trained strength
reserve_volunteer_trained.description: Army Reserve Future Reserves 2020 trained strength (completed Phase 1 or higher), including 615 already mobilised and 1,720 on Full Time Reserve Service.
reserve_volunteer_trained.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 6a

reserve_volunteer_deployable_fraction.label: Reservists who actually deploy
reserve_volunteer_deployable_fraction.description: Share of the trained Army Reserve that reports, passes medical and is available on call-out.
reserve_volunteer_deployable_fraction.source: Derived from House of Commons Defence Committee, Lessons of Iraq, Third Report of Session 2003-04, HC 57-I, chapter 5 (Use of Reserves); MoD Service Personnel Statistics, 1 July 2026, Table 6a
reserve_volunteer_deployable_fraction.derivation: Two stages. Structural: of 23,517 trained Army Reserve (SPS Table 6a), 1,720 are on full-time reserve service and 615 already mobilised, leaving 0.901 of the strength available to be served a notice. Empirical: 0.579 of notices served were accepted into service on Operation Telic 1. 0.901 x 0.579 = 0.522, held at 0.50.
reserve_volunteer_deployable_fraction.note: This was an assumption of 0.50 reasoned from the composition of the trained figure; Operation Telic gives the first primary measurement of the same quantity and puts it at 0.52, so the value is unchanged and its standing is not. Held at 0.50 rather than raised to 0.52 because the Telic denominator had already been filtered for expected wastage (HC 57 paragraph 112) and because the trained figure has counted Phase-1-only personnel since October 2016 (SPS note 32), neither of which the two stages above capture. Both push the true figure below 0.522, not above it.

reserve_mobilisation_acceptance_rate.label: Reservists accepted per call-out notice
reserve_mobilisation_acceptance_rate.description: Share of Army reservists served a compulsory call-out notice who were accepted into service, after non-reporting, medical failure and exemption.
reserve_mobilisation_acceptance_rate.source: Derived from House of Commons Defence Committee, Lessons of Iraq, Third Report of Session 2003-04, HC 57-I, chapter 5 (Use of Reserves)
reserve_mobilisation_acceptance_rate.derivation: Operation Telic 1, Army, HC 57 Table 1: 3,787 accepted into service / 6,540 call-out notices served = 0.579. Tri-service the same table gives 5,221 / 8,492 = 0.615.
reserve_mobilisation_acceptance_rate.note: The denominator is notices served, not the trained reserve: HC 57 paragraph 112 records that MoD made allowance for expected wastage before deciding whom to serve. The rate therefore sits downstream of a list that had already been filtered.

reserve_exemption_application_rate.label: Call-out notices contested
reserve_exemption_application_rate.description: Share of call-out notices that produced an application for exemption or deferral, from the reservist or the employer.
reserve_exemption_application_rate.source: Derived from House of Commons Defence Committee, Lessons of Iraq, Third Report of Session 2003-04, HC 57-I, chapter 5 (Use of Reserves)
reserve_exemption_application_rate.derivation: Operation Telic 1, HC 57 paragraph 113: 2,021 applications for exemption + 80 for deferral = 2,101, against 8,492 notices served (Table 1) = 0.247.

reserve_exemption_employer_share.label: Exemption applications made by employers
reserve_exemption_employer_share.description: Share of applications for exemption from call-out that came from the reservist's employer rather than the reservist.
reserve_exemption_employer_share.source: Derived from House of Commons Defence Committee, Lessons of Iraq, Third Report of Session 2003-04, HC 57-I, chapter 5 (Use of Reserves)
reserve_exemption_employer_share.derivation: Operation Telic 1, HC 57 paragraph 113: of 2,021 applications for exemption, 920 were from employers and 1,101 from reservists. 920 / 2,021 = 0.455.

reserve_medical_fail_ex_regular.label: Ex-regulars failing the mobilisation medical
reserve_medical_fail_ex_regular.description: Share of Regular Reserve personnel who reported to the mobilisation centre and failed the medical.
reserve_medical_fail_ex_regular.source: House of Commons Defence Committee, Lessons of Iraq, Third Report of Session 2003-04, HC 57-I, chapter 5 (Use of Reserves)
reserve_medical_fail_ex_regular.note: HC 57 paragraph 119, on the Reserves Training and Mobilisation Centre at Chilwell. The Committee recommended MoD consider how to return these reservists to being fit for role.

reserve_medical_fail_volunteer.label: Volunteer reservists failing the mobilisation medical
reserve_medical_fail_volunteer.description: Share of Territorial Army personnel who reported to the mobilisation centre and failed the medical.
reserve_medical_fail_volunteer.source: House of Commons Defence Committee, Lessons of Iraq, Third Report of Session 2003-04, HC 57-I, chapter 5 (Use of Reserves)
reserve_medical_fail_volunteer.note: HC 57 paragraph 119. The 48% / 14% gap between the ex-regular and volunteer reserves is the only primary measurement of that asymmetry the model has.

reserve_notice_days_default.label: Army Reserve call-out notice
reserve_notice_days_default.description: Planning assumption for the notice period under which the Army Reserve is warned for call-out under Reserve Forces Act 1996 s.52.
reserve_notice_days_default.source: Armed Forces Bill 2026, amendment papers (Select Committee, 14–15 Apr 2026): Army Reserve Group A standard notice is readiness category R9 (180 days)
reserve_notice_days_default.derivation: Readiness category R9 = 180 days, as stated in the amendment text; the Act itself sets no fixed period.

reserve_notice_days_amended.label: Amended call-out notice
reserve_notice_days_amended.description: Notice period if the 90-day amendment is legislated.
reserve_notice_days_amended.source: Armed Forces Bill 2026, amendment 24 (Public Bill Committee, sixth sitting, 16 Apr 2026): proposed reduction to R8 (90 days)
reserve_notice_days_amended.derivation: Proposed amendment, not enacted; the Government's reply was that readiness levels are reviewed annually.

reserve_arrival_months_default.label: Reservist arrival, default notice
reserve_arrival_months_default.description: Months from call-out to reservists counting toward Force Ready at 180 days' notice, including a short refresher.
reserve_arrival_months_default.source: Derived from the standard call-out notice period
reserve_arrival_months_default.derivation: 180 days ≈ 6 months; refresher assumed to overlap with the notice period.

reserve_arrival_months_amended.label: Reservist arrival, 90-day notice
reserve_arrival_months_amended.description: Months from call-out to reservists counting toward Force Ready at 90 days' notice.
reserve_arrival_months_amended.source: Derived from the amended call-out notice period

ex_regular_tracked.label: Army Regular Reserve on record
ex_regular_tracked.description: Army ex-regulars with a recall liability who appear on current records (Reserve Land Forces, Regular Reserve). The tri-service figure of 34,755 includes Royal Navy and RAF veterans who would not be soldiers in a division. The 1 July 2026 figure is marked estimated in the source; 1 April 2026 is used.
ex_regular_tracked.source: MoD, UK armed forces quarterly service personnel statistics: 1 July 2026, Table 8a

ex_regular_delay_months.label: Ex-regular recall delay
ex_regular_delay_months.description: Months from recall order to the first ex-regulars reporting.
ex_regular_delay_months.rationale: Recall notices must be served at recorded addresses; the game allows 2–4 months.

ex_regular_report_ceiling.label: Ex-regulars who ever report
ex_regular_report_ceiling.description: Share of the tracked Ex-Regular Reserve who are located, fit and report over the course of the game.
ex_regular_report_ceiling.rationale: The MoD has acknowledged that address records for the Regular Reserve are incomplete; medical and age exemptions remove more. Now an upper bound rather than a central estimate: the medical failure rate for ex-regulars who actually reported is 0.48 (HC 57 paragraph 119), so the medical alone leaves 0.52 before any allowance for records or age. Lowering it would be a balance change, and has not been made.

ex_regular_report_rate_monthly.label: Ex-regular monthly reporting rate
ex_regular_report_rate_monthly.description: Share of the not-yet-reported (but reportable) ex-regulars who report each month after the delay.
ex_regular_report_rate_monthly.rationale: Geometric arrival; most of those who will report do so within six months.

strategic_reserve_claimed.label: Strategic Reserve, as claimed
strategic_reserve_claimed.description: Size of the ex-regular 'Strategic Reserve' as publicly stated by ministers in early 2026.
strategic_reserve_claimed.source: MoD press release, 15 Jan 2026 (recall age raised to 65) and Forces News, 15 Jan 2026: 'an estimated 95,000 people have a Strategic Reservist liability'
strategic_reserve_claimed.derivation: Ministerial estimate as reported; the MoD's own impact assessment (27 Feb 2026) says efforts to improve contact information are under way.

strategic_reserve_untracked.label: Strategic Reserve not on record, Army share
strategic_reserve_untracked.description: Claimed Strategic Reserve less the Ex-Regular Reserve on record, scaled to the Army's share of the Regular Reserve.
strategic_reserve_untracked.source: Derived from the claimed Strategic Reserve and the Ex-Regular Reserve on record

strategic_trace_delay_months.label: Strategic Reserve trace time
strategic_trace_delay_months.description: Months from ordering a trace of the untracked Strategic Reserve to the traced pool reporting.
strategic_trace_delay_months.rationale: Matching against HMRC, DWP and electoral records takes months and has never been exercised at scale.

strategic_trace_yield_min.label: Trace yield, low
strategic_trace_yield_min.description: Lower bound on the share of the untracked Strategic Reserve located by a trace.

strategic_trace_yield_max.label: Trace yield, high
strategic_trace_yield_max.description: Upper bound on the share of the untracked Strategic Reserve located by a trace.

strategic_report_fraction.label: Traced ex-regulars who report
strategic_report_fraction.description: Share of the traced Strategic Reserve who are fit, under the age limit and actually report.
strategic_report_fraction.rationale: Many will be over recall age or medically unfit; none have trained for years.

uk_population_scaling.description: Multiplier applied to England and Wales age bands to approximate the UK, assuming Scotland and Northern Ireland share the same age profile.
uk_population_scaling.source: ONS: UK mid-2025 provisional (69,487,000) and England and Wales mid-2025 (62,010,000)

women_included_support_pct.label: Public support for including women
women_included_support_pct.description: Share of the public who say women should be included in any conscription.
women_included_support_pct.source: YouGov daily results, 26 Jan 2024: should women be conscripted on the same basis as men (42%) or with some restrictions (30%)

willingness_start_pct.label: Willingness to serve
willingness_start_pct.description: Share of adults who say they would be willing to serve if conscription were introduced.
willingness_start_pct.source: YouGov, July 2026, as reported 23 Jul 2026: 6% would volunteer, 14% would serve if conscripted
willingness_start_pct.derivation: 6 + 14 = 20. YouGov's own results page could not be located; figures are from secondary reporting.

self_declared_ineligible_pct.label: Self-declared ineligible
self_declared_ineligible_pct.description: Share of adults who say they would be ineligible to serve on health or other grounds.
self_declared_ineligible_pct.source: YouGov, July 2026, as reported 23 Jul 2026: 52% say they would be ineligible on health or age grounds
self_declared_ineligible_pct.derivation: Secondary reporting; used for flavour only.

conscription_willingness_adj_18_25.label: Willingness adjustment, band 18-25
conscription_willingness_adj_18_25.description: Points added to public willingness when the Bill conscripts ages 18-25, relative to the default 18-30 band.
conscription_willingness_adj_18_25.source: Derived from YouGov, 4,205 GB adults, 28 May 2024: "Would you support or oppose it being made compulsory for all young people to either serve in the military for a year or spend one weekend every month for a year community volunteering?"; ONS, Estimates of the population for England and Wales, mid-2025 (MYE2)
conscription_willingness_adj_18_25.derivation: Support (strongly + somewhat) by YouGov age group -- 18-24: 27%, 25-49: 39%, 50-64: 53%, 65+: 63% -- weighted by the England and Wales population of each single year of age inside the band gives 28.58% for 18-25, against 32.84% for 18-30. Difference rounded to whole points.
conscription_willingness_adj_18_25.note: The question offers military service OR community volunteering, so its absolute level overstates support for military-only conscription. Only the age gradient is used; the level stays anchored to willingness_start_pct. Every band this game offers starts at 18, so all of them contain the most hostile group and widening only dilutes it: the whole range from 18-25 to 18-65 is 13 points. See docs/design-review.md F14.

conscription_willingness_adj_18_30.label: Willingness adjustment, band 18-30
conscription_willingness_adj_18_30.description: Points added to public willingness when the Bill conscripts ages 18-30, relative to the default 18-30 band.
conscription_willingness_adj_18_30.source: Derived from YouGov, 4,205 GB adults, 28 May 2024: "Would you support or oppose it being made compulsory for all young people to either serve in the military for a year or spend one weekend every month for a year community volunteering?"; ONS, Estimates of the population for England and Wales, mid-2025 (MYE2)
conscription_willingness_adj_18_30.derivation: Support (strongly + somewhat) by YouGov age group -- 18-24: 27%, 25-49: 39%, 50-64: 53%, 65+: 63% -- weighted by the England and Wales population of each single year of age inside the band gives 32.84% for 18-30, against 32.84% for 18-30. Difference rounded to whole points.
conscription_willingness_adj_18_30.note: The question offers military service OR community volunteering, so its absolute level overstates support for military-only conscription. Only the age gradient is used; the level stays anchored to willingness_start_pct. Every band this game offers starts at 18, so all of them contain the most hostile group and widening only dilutes it: the whole range from 18-25 to 18-65 is 13 points. See docs/design-review.md F14.

conscription_willingness_adj_26_40.label: Willingness adjustment, band 26-40
conscription_willingness_adj_26_40.description: Points added to public willingness when the Bill conscripts ages 26-40, relative to the default 18-30 band.
conscription_willingness_adj_26_40.source: Derived from YouGov, 4,205 GB adults, 28 May 2024: "Would you support or oppose it being made compulsory for all young people to either serve in the military for a year or spend one weekend every month for a year community volunteering?"; ONS, Estimates of the population for England and Wales, mid-2025 (MYE2)
conscription_willingness_adj_26_40.derivation: Every single year of age from 26 to 40 falls inside YouGov's 25-49 group, so the population-weighted support for this band is that group's figure exactly: 39.0%, against 32.84% for 18-30. Difference 6.15, rounded to whole points. Checked against the other bands by subtraction: (35.68 x 18,665,415 - 28.58 x 5,938,195) / 12,727,220 = 38.99%, which is the same figure. This is the only band the Bill offers whose lower bound is not 18, and therefore the only one that does not contain the most hostile age group (18-24, 27% support, 45% strongly opposed).

conscription_willingness_adj_18_65.label: Willingness adjustment, band 18-65
conscription_willingness_adj_18_65.description: Points added to public willingness when the Bill conscripts ages 18-65, relative to the default 18-30 band.
conscription_willingness_adj_18_65.source: Derived from YouGov, 4,205 GB adults, 28 May 2024: "Would you support or oppose it being made compulsory for all young people to either serve in the military for a year or spend one weekend every month for a year community volunteering?"; ONS, Estimates of the population for England and Wales, mid-2025 (MYE2)
conscription_willingness_adj_18_65.derivation: Support (strongly + somewhat) by YouGov age group -- 18-24: 27%, 25-49: 39%, 50-64: 53%, 65+: 63% -- weighted by the England and Wales population of each single year of age inside the band gives 42.16% for 18-65, against 32.84% for 18-30. Difference rounded to whole points.
conscription_willingness_adj_18_65.note: The question offers military service OR community volunteering, so its absolute level overstates support for military-only conscription. Only the age gradient is used; the level stays anchored to willingness_start_pct. Every band this game offers starts at 18, so all of them contain the most hostile group and widening only dilutes it: the whole range from 18-25 to 18-65 is 13 points. See docs/design-review.md F14.

refusal_strong_opposition_intercept.label: Strong opposition at zero willingness
refusal_strong_opposition_intercept.description: Intercept of the fitted line from public willingness to the share who strongly oppose compulsory service.
refusal_strong_opposition_intercept.source: Derived from YouGov, 4,205 GB adults, 28 May 2024: "Would you support or oppose it being made compulsory for all young people to either serve in the military for a year or spend one weekend every month for a year community volunteering?"
refusal_strong_opposition_intercept.derivation: Least squares on YouGov's four age groups, (support%, strongly oppose%) = (27,45), (39,37), (53,24), (63,18): strongly oppose = 66.206 - 0.7738 x support, R2 = 0.994.
refusal_strong_opposition_intercept.note: Used below the polled range: the game's willingness runs 16-34 where the poll observed 27-63, so the figures it produces (roughly 40-54% strongly opposed) sit at and beyond the most hostile group YouGov measured. That is an extrapolation, and it is the weakest link in this chain.

refusal_strong_opposition_slope.label: Strong opposition per point of willingness
refusal_strong_opposition_slope.description: Points of strong opposition removed by each point of public willingness.
refusal_strong_opposition_slope.source: Derived from YouGov, 4,205 GB adults, 28 May 2024: "Would you support or oppose it being made compulsory for all young people to either serve in the military for a year or spend one weekend every month for a year community volunteering?"
refusal_strong_opposition_slope.derivation: Slope of the same least-squares fit as the intercept above.

conscription_refusal_conversion.label: Strong opponents who refuse the call-up
conscription_refusal_conversion.description: Share of those who strongly oppose compulsory service who fail to report when called.
conscription_refusal_conversion.rationale: Saying you strongly oppose a policy is not the same as breaking the law when it applies to you, and most people comply. The nearest measurement the project has is HC 57: 25.5% of Army reservists served a compulsory call-out notice on Operation Telic did not report -- and those were volunteers who had signed up. A quarter of strong opponents gives 11-14% of a conscript intake failing to report, which is below that reservist figure and above zero.

medical_pass_peacetime.label: Medical pass rate, peacetime standard
medical_pass_peacetime.description: Share of the called-up cohort passing the peacetime entry medical.
medical_pass_peacetime.rationale: Medical rejection is the single largest reason Army applicants fail; about half of adults say they would be ineligible.

medical_pass_relaxed.label: Medical pass rate, relaxed standard
medical_pass_relaxed.description: Share of the called-up cohort passing a relaxed entry medical.

medical_pass_wartime.label: Medical pass rate, wartime standard
medical_pass_wartime.description: Share of the called-up cohort passing a wartime entry medical.

exemption_strict.label: Exempted share, strict regime
exemption_strict.description: Share of the age band exempted under a reserved-occupations-only regime.
exemption_strict.source: Modelling assumption (1939 Schedule of Reserved Occupations as comparator)

exemption_broad.label: Exempted share, broad regime
exemption_broad.description: Share of the age band exempted when students, carers and key workers are added.

exemption_minimal.label: Exempted share, minimal regime
exemption_minimal.description: Share of the age band exempted under a minimal regime.

bill_months_emergency.label: National Service Bill, emergency procedure
bill_months_emergency.description: Months for a National Service Bill to pass under an emergency timetable.
bill_months_emergency.source: Modelling assumption (Armed Forces Bill timetable as comparator)

bill_months_normal.label: National Service Bill, normal procedure
bill_months_normal.description: Months for a National Service Bill to pass under the normal timetable.
bill_months_normal.source: Modelling assumption (Armed Forces Bill timetable as comparator)

phase1_weeks.label: Phase 1 training length
phase1_weeks.description: Length of Phase 1 (basic) training for Army other ranks.
phase1_weeks.source: House of Lords written question HL1629, answered 26 Feb 2020: Phase 1 at ATC Pirbright is 14 weeks
phase1_weeks.derivation: Common Military Syllabus length as stated in the answer.

phase2_weeks.label: Phase 2 training length, average
phase2_weeks.description: Average length of Phase 2 (trade) training across Army trades.
phase2_weeks.source: Modelling assumption; Army recruiting material gives Phase 2 as 15–27 weeks depending on trade (infantry 10)
phase2_weeks.rationale: Mid-point of the published 15–27 week range. HL1629 gives no average; Phase 2 length varies by trade.

phase1_weeks_compressed.label: Phase 1, compressed
phase1_weeks_compressed.description: Phase 1 length under a compressed wartime syllabus.

phase2_weeks_compressed.label: Phase 2, compressed
phase2_weeks_compressed.description: Average Phase 2 length under a compressed wartime syllabus.

syllabus_throughput_multiplier.label: Compressed syllabus throughput
syllabus_throughput_multiplier.description: Multiplier on training capacity when the syllabus is compressed (same instructors, shorter courses).

compressed_effectiveness_penalty.label: Compressed syllabus effectiveness penalty
compressed_effectiveness_penalty.description: Reduction in graduate effectiveness under the compressed syllabus.

attrition_compressed_add.label: Extra attrition, compressed syllabus
attrition_compressed_add.description: Percentage points added to training attrition under the compressed syllabus.

attrition_wartime_medical_add.label: Extra attrition, wartime medical standard
attrition_wartime_medical_add.description: Percentage points added to training attrition when the wartime medical standard admits less fit recruits.

attrition_relaxed_medical_add.label: Extra attrition, relaxed medical standard
attrition_relaxed_medical_add.description: Percentage points added to training attrition under the relaxed medical standard.

attrition_age_add_18_25.label: Extra attrition, age band 18-25
attrition_age_add_18_25.description: Percentage points added to training attrition for conscript cohorts raised under a 18-25 age band.
attrition_age_add_18_25.rationale: Basic training is designed around entrants of this age, and the training attrition rate is measured on an intake that is overwhelmingly this age, so the default band carries no adjustment. Zero as the reference.

attrition_age_add_18_30.label: Extra attrition, age band 18-30
attrition_age_add_18_30.description: Percentage points added to training attrition for conscript cohorts raised under a 18-30 age band.
attrition_age_add_18_30.rationale: The default band, and the reference point. The training attrition rate (0.26) is measured on the Army's actual untrained intake, which sits inside it. Zero by construction.

attrition_age_add_26_40.label: Extra attrition, age band 26-40
attrition_age_add_26_40.description: Percentage points added to training attrition for conscript cohorts raised under a 26-40 age band.
attrition_age_add_26_40.rationale: No figure for British Army training attrition by age at entry is published: the quarterly service personnel statistics give untrained intake and outflow but do not break either by age, so this is a frank assumption rather than a derivation, in the way the refusal conversion is. What it stands for is real and one-directional - a recruit in their thirties is more likely to be injured, medically downgraded or to leave for reasons outside training than one at 19 - and it is set at 5 points against a base of 26 because that is the same order as the relaxed medical standard's 4 points and below the wartime standard's 10, which are the two comparable adjustments already in the model. It exists because it is the only place an older band's cost can actually land: it charges throughput, where the medical standard and the exemptions regime only resize an eligible pool that never binds. Replace it if attrition by age at entry is ever published.

attrition_age_add_18_65.label: Extra attrition, age band 18-65
attrition_age_add_18_65.description: Percentage points added to training attrition for conscript cohorts raised under a 18-65 age band.
attrition_age_add_18_65.rationale: The same assumption as the 26-40 band's, weighted down because this band is mostly younger people: two thirds of the 18-65 population is under 45, so the band's mean age at entry is below 26-40's even though its upper bound is far higher.

capacity_purchase_annual.label: Capacity per purchase
capacity_purchase_annual.description: Additional annual trained output per training-capacity purchase.
capacity_purchase_annual.rationale: Roughly one additional Phase 1 training centre.

capacity_standup_months.label: Capacity stand-up time
capacity_standup_months.description: Months from purchasing training capacity to it accepting recruits.

capacity_purchase_cost.label: Capacity purchase cost
capacity_purchase_cost.description: One-off cost of each +5,000/yr block of training capacity (estate, ranges, accommodation).
capacity_purchase_cost.rationale: Game design; excludes the instructors, who are diverted rather than hired.

civilian_instructor_capacity_annual.label: Civilian instructor capacity
civilian_instructor_capacity_annual.description: Additional annual trained output from contracted civilian instructors, non-combat trades only, without drawing on junior leaders.

civilian_instructor_delay_months.label: Civilian instructor lead time
civilian_instructor_delay_months.description: Months to contract and stand up civilian instructors.

civilian_instructor_cost_annual.label: Civilian instructor contract cost
civilian_instructor_cost_annual.description: Annual cost of the civilian instructor contract.
civilian_instructor_cost_annual.rationale: About 250 instructors at a fully loaded £60k each.

equipment_cost_per_head.label: Personal equipment per conscript
equipment_cost_per_head.description: One-off cost of personal kit (clothing, body armour, helmet, rifle, load-carrying equipment) per conscript.
equipment_cost_per_head.source: Modelling assumption. The brief's citations (Absolute Military, Mar 2026; Defence Investment Plan, 30 Jun 2026) could not be verified; Phase 1 clothing alone was £2,000 per recruit in FY2023-24
equipment_cost_per_head.rationale: £2,000 of clothing plus body armour, helmet, rifle and load-carrying equipment; a £3.5–5k range is retained as plausible.

equipment_lead_months.label: Equipment lead time
equipment_lead_months.description: Months from placing an emergency equipment order to kit being issued.
equipment_lead_months.source: Modelling assumption, against NAO, The Equipment Plan 2023-2033 (HC 315, Session 2023-24, 4 December 2023), paragraphs 2.5 and 2.20
equipment_lead_months.rationale: Game design. The NAO puts the evidence against it: a decade of "lean" stockpiles and "just in time" delivery of spares has left no buffer to draw on, the MoD has had to earmark more than £5 billion over ten years to re-establish war holdings, and it records that "the lead time for replenishing stock and establishing war holdings presents challenges" (HC 315 para 2.20). The Army separately told the NAO that semiconductor lead times had gone from one to three weeks to more than fifty (para 2.5), though that is components rather than the clothing, body armour, helmet and rifle this parameter buys. Four months is therefore the optimistic end of the range, not the middle, and the range is widened upward to say so. Not raised, because moving it is a balance change and the NAO figures are not measurements of this quantity.

junior_entry_attrition.label: Junior entry attrition
junior_entry_attrition.description: Share of Army Foundation College (Harrogate) junior entrants who do not complete.
junior_entry_attrition.source: Forces News, 13 Nov 2025: AFC Harrogate non-completion averaged 34% over 2018–2023, the highest of any Army training establishment
junior_entry_attrition.derivation: 2018–2023 average as reported. The course itself is 49 weeks (long) or 23 weeks (short); the two-year lead is set by the minimum deployment age.

junior_entry_lead_months.label: Junior entry lead time
junior_entry_lead_months.description: Months from enrolling a 16-year-old junior entrant to a deployable 18-year-old soldier.
junior_entry_lead_months.source: Derived from the minimum deployment age of 18
junior_entry_lead_months.derivation: UK policy: under-18s are not deployed on operations. Entry at 16 implies a two-year lead.

vetting_throughput_monthly.label: Vetting clearances a month
vetting_throughput_monthly.description: Ceiling on how many people can be called up in a month while the security vetting queue is congested. Nobody enters training without a clearance, so this bounds the call-up regardless of what the training estate could take.
vetting_throughput_monthly.source: Modelling assumption. UKSV scale and the fact of chronic congestion from NAO, Investigation into the performance of UK Security Vetting (January 2023); the ceiling itself is a game figure, not an NAO one.
vetting_throughput_monthly.rationale: The share of UKSV throughput the Army could expect during a congestion, against a service that handles roughly fifteen thousand clearances a month across all of government. Sized so the ceiling is invisible on the baseline training estate (spare intake of a few dozen a month) and binding once capacity has been bought (spare intake 2,900-4,900).

vetting_rescreen_throughput_monthly.label: Vetting clearances a month while re-screening
vetting_rescreen_throughput_monthly.description: The tighter ceiling that applies while every recruit cleared under a lowered standard is screened again. Re-screening consumes the same teams that clear new applicants.
vetting_rescreen_throughput_monthly.source: Modelling assumption. UKSV scale and the fact of chronic congestion from NAO, Investigation into the performance of UK Security Vetting (January 2023); the ceiling itself is a game figure, not an NAO one.
vetting_rescreen_throughput_monthly.rationale: Three-quarters of the ordinary congested throughput: re-screening work competes with new clearances for the same officers, so a review of past cases costs roughly a quarter of current capacity.

eff_regular.label: Effectiveness: regular, trade-trained
eff_regular.description: Reference effectiveness of a trade-trained regular soldier in a formed unit.

eff_reserve_volunteer.label: Effectiveness: volunteer reservist
eff_reserve_volunteer.description: Effectiveness of a trained Army Reservist after a refresher period.
eff_reserve_volunteer.rationale: Trained, but with fewer collective-training days per year than regulars.

eff_ex_regular.label: Effectiveness: ex-regular, recalled
eff_ex_regular.description: Effectiveness of a recalled ex-regular on the tracked Regular Reserve.
eff_ex_regular.rationale: Formerly fully trained; skills fade and fitness declines over the years since leaving.

eff_strategic.label: Effectiveness: Strategic Reserve, traced
eff_strategic.description: Effectiveness of a traced member of the untracked Strategic Reserve.
eff_strategic.rationale: Longer out of service than the tracked reserve, on average.

eff_conscript_normal_start.label: Effectiveness: conscript at graduation, normal syllabus
eff_conscript_normal_start.description: Effectiveness of an equipped conscript on completing the full 34-week syllabus.
eff_conscript_normal_start.rationale: Trade-trained but with no collective training and no experience.

eff_conscript_normal_cap.label: Effectiveness cap: conscript, normal syllabus
eff_conscript_normal_cap.description: Maximum effectiveness a normal-syllabus conscript reaches through collective training.

eff_conscript_compressed_start.label: Effectiveness: conscript at graduation, compressed syllabus
eff_conscript_compressed_start.description: Effectiveness of an equipped conscript on completing the compressed 22-week syllabus.
eff_conscript_compressed_start.rationale: Normal-syllabus start less the compressed-syllabus penalty.

eff_conscript_compressed_cap.label: Effectiveness cap: conscript, compressed syllabus
eff_conscript_compressed_cap.description: Maximum effectiveness a compressed-syllabus conscript reaches through collective training.

eff_conscript_growth_monthly.label: Conscript effectiveness growth
eff_conscript_growth_monthly.description: Effectiveness gained per month of collective training after graduation.

eff_conscript_unequipped.label: Effectiveness: conscript, trained, unequipped
eff_conscript_unequipped.description: Effectiveness of a trained conscript without personal equipment.

regular_pay_annual.label: Regular soldier pay, entry rate
regular_pay_annual.description: Annual pay of an Other Rank at the initial pay point (OR2-01), including X-Factor, from 1 April 2026.
regular_pay_annual.source: Armed Forces' Pay Review Body, Fifty-Fifth Report 2026, Appendix 1 Table 1.1

pension_employer_multiplier.label: Pay to employer-cost multiplier
pension_employer_multiplier.description: Multiplier converting pay into employer cost, using the Armed Forces Pension Scheme employer contribution rate of 73.5%.
pension_employer_multiplier.source: Armed Forces Pension Scheme annual accounts 2024–25: employer contributions paid at 73.5% of pensionable pay
pension_employer_multiplier.derivation: 1 + 0.735. The 2024 valuation reduces the rate to 52.3% from 1 April 2027.

conscript_pay_annual.label: Conscript pay
conscript_pay_annual.description: Annual pay of a conscript in training, set at the National Living Wage for a 37.5-hour week.

training_cost_per_recruit.label: Phase 1 training cost per recruit
training_cost_per_recruit.description: Cost of Phase 1 training per recruit at ATC Pirbright, FY2023-24. Phase 2 costs vary by trade and are not included, so this understates the true cost.
training_cost_per_recruit.source: Written answer (Luke Pollard MP to James Cartlidge MP), FY2023-24, as reported by UK Defence Journal, 22 Oct 2024
training_cost_per_recruit.derivation: Figure as reported; the parliamentary question reference could not be located. HL1629 gave £38,000 in 2020.

reservist_award_annual.label: Reservist Award top-up
reservist_award_annual.description: Average annual Reservist Award paid to mobilised reservists to make up civilian salary.
reservist_award_annual.rationale: The award covers the gap between civilian and military pay; the average is not published.

employer_assistance_daily.label: Employer financial assistance
employer_assistance_daily.description: Daily payment to a mobilised reservist's employer under the Reserve Forces (Call-out and Recall) (Financial Assistance) Regulations 2005.
employer_assistance_daily.source: Reserve Forces (Call-out and Recall) (Financial Assistance) Regulations 2005, SI 2005/859, regulation 6(3)
employer_assistance_daily.derivation: Cap on the employer's award as made; later amendments not checked.

cost_pc_allowance_per_month.label: Treasury allowance per month of the campaign
cost_pc_allowance_per_month.description: Cumulative Treasury cost the mobilisation may run up per month of its deadline before the Treasury starts charging political capital. The allowance for a run is this figure times the difficulty's deadline in months.
cost_pc_allowance_per_month.rationale: Replaces a flat £5bn threshold that could not fire at Brigade or Division and fired once at Corps. The Treasury's tolerance is a budget voted for an operation, and a longer operation is voted a bigger one, so the allowance is sized to the campaign rather than fixed: 4 months buys £0.8bn, 12 months £2.4bn, 24 months £4.8bn. The level is anchored on the defence budget: £200m is 3.9% of one month of the 2025/26 defence budget (£5.19bn), the order of in-year flexibility a department can absorb before the Treasury takes an interest; the range runs 1.9% to 7.7% of a month's defence budget. A flat threshold cannot do this job at all, because it is charged every month against a total that only grows: measured over 40 seeds, lowering the flat figure far enough to charge the sensible strategy 6 political capital across a Division run charged it 36 across a Corps one. Two properties fixed the level inside the range. Below about £175m Corps gets materially harder than it is meant to be: a maximum-effort programme resigns on 35-40% of seeds rather than 18%. And the Equipment Plan's contingency must stay worth less than one whole step at Corps (£4.1bn against an allowance of £4.8bn = 0.85 steps, where the old flat £5bn gave 0.82), or drawing the contingency wins everywhere and the fork that action exists for closes. Above about £250m the mechanic is dormant at every rung, which is where it was.

cost_pc_penalty_per_step.label: Cost penalty per allowance step
cost_pc_penalty_per_step.description: Political capital lost per turn for each whole Treasury allowance of cumulative cost run up.
cost_pc_penalty_per_step.rationale: Game design. The quantity it multiplies changed from a flat £5bn threshold to an allowance sized to the campaign; the charge per step did not.

defence_budget_2025.label: Defence budget 2025/26
defence_budget_2025.description: Ministry of Defence total departmental expenditure limit, 2025/26, used as the denominator for cost percentages.
defence_budget_2025.source: MoD Supplementary Estimate memorandum 2025-26: RDEL £47,388.7m + CDEL £23,067.1m
defence_budget_2025.derivation: 47,388.7 + 23,067.1 = £62,455.8m, reported as £62.3bn in the Commons Library briefing CBP-8175; the rounded figure is used.

equipment_plan_deficit.label: Equipment Plan funding deficit
equipment_plan_deficit.description: Amount by which the Ministry of Defence's own forecast costs for the ten-year Equipment Plan exceed its budget.
equipment_plan_deficit.source: NAO, The Equipment Plan 2023-2033, HC 315, Session 2023-24, 4 December 2023
equipment_plan_deficit.note: Forecast costs £305.5bn against a budget of £288.6bn over ten years, which the NAO records as the largest deficit since it began reporting on the Plan. The Equipment Plan is reported annually and a 2026 edition would supersede this one; the figure is used because it is the most recent the project has been given, and because the Chancellor in this game would be quoting the last published audit rather than an unpublished one.

defence_budget_deficit_10yr.label: Ten-year defence budget deficit
defence_budget_deficit_10yr.description: Amount by which forecast spending across the whole defence budget exceeds it over ten years.
defence_budget_deficit_10yr.source: NAO, The Equipment Plan 2023-2033, HC 315, Session 2023-24, 4 December 2023
defence_budget_deficit_10yr.note: Against a £4.3bn shortfall the year before. All six Top Level Budgets forecast costs above their ten-year budgets. The Equipment Plan is reported annually and a 2026 edition would supersede this one; the figure is used because it is the most recent the project has been given, and because the Chancellor in this game would be quoting the last published audit rather than an unpublished one.

army_capability_gap.label: The Army's own stated capability gap
army_capability_gap.description: Further funding the Army estimated it could need to provide in full the capability it is committed to.
army_capability_gap.source: NAO, The Equipment Plan 2023-2033, HC 315, Session 2023-24, 4 December 2023
army_capability_gap.note: Reported by the NAO as the Army's own estimate, alongside a declared Army deficit of £1.2bn for the year. It is the number that makes the Chancellor's letter in this game a quotation rather than an invention. The Equipment Plan is reported annually and a 2026 edition would supersede this one; the figure is used because it is the most recent the project has been given, and because the Chancellor in this game would be quoting the last published audit rather than an unpublished one.

equipment_plan_contingency.label: Contingency held in the Equipment Plan
equipment_plan_contingency.description: Money set aside inside the Equipment Plan to fund new equipment projects or absorb unexpected cost increases.
equipment_plan_contingency.source: NAO, The Equipment Plan 2023-2033, HC 315, Session 2023-24, 4 December 2023, paragraph 1.9
equipment_plan_contingency.note: Down from £4.3bn the year before and £5.9bn in 2021. It is the only pot in the NAO's account that a minister could plausibly reach for at short notice, and it is the buffer the Plan relies on, which is what makes spending it a decision rather than a windfall.

contingency_drawn_penalty_add.label: Extra Treasury charge once the buffer is gone
contingency_drawn_penalty_add.description: Added to the political capital charged for each step of cumulative cost, once the Equipment Plan's contingency has been spent.
contingency_drawn_penalty_add.rationale: The contingency exists to absorb unexpected cost increases (NAO 1.9). Spend it on the mobilisation and every subsequent overrun lands on the Plan instead of on the buffer, so the Treasury's tolerance narrows. Doubling the charge per step rather than adding one to it, because the crossover has to sit inside the spend the game actually produces: a full Corps run costs £4.6-11.1bn, so at +1 the draw was better everywhere and the decision was no decision. At +2 the draw wins while it clears your only step of Treasury pressure and loses from the second step on — crossover at about £9bn of cumulative cost, which sits between what a restrained Corps programme spends (6.8) and what an all-out one spends (9.7).

contingency_equipment_delay_months.label: Equipment slip after the contingency is spent
contingency_equipment_delay_months.description: Months added to the emergency equipment order when the Equipment Plan's contingency has been spent on the mobilisation instead.
contingency_equipment_delay_months.rationale: The contingency's first stated purpose is to fund new equipment projects (NAO 1.9); an emergency order for tens of thousands of sets is exactly that. Spent elsewhere, the order joins the queue rather than jumping it. Three months against an equipment lead time of four roughly doubles the wait, which is the right order of magnitude for losing your place in a programme the NAO already describes as delay-prone.

uk_gdp_2025.label: UK GDP 2025
uk_gdp_2025.description: UK nominal GDP for calendar 2025, used as the denominator for GDP-loss percentages.
uk_gdp_2025.source: ONS, GDP at current market prices, 2025 (series YBHA)

output_per_worker_labour_share.label: Output per worker, labour share
output_per_worker_labour_share.description: Annual GDP lost per person removed from the civilian workforce, counting only the labour share of output.
output_per_worker_labour_share.source: ONS: compensation of employees 2025 (DTWM, £1,511.5bn) divided by employees (MGRN, 29.59m)
output_per_worker_labour_share.derivation: 1,511,529 / 29,590 ≈ £51,100 per employee. The brief's £53k could not be reproduced.

output_per_worker_gross.label: Output per worker, gross
output_per_worker_gross.description: Annual GDP per worker, gross. Shown as the alternative to the labour-share figure.

gdp_age_multiplier_18_25.label: Output multiplier, 18–25
gdp_age_multiplier_18_25.description: Output per worker in the 18–25 band relative to the all-age average.
gdp_age_multiplier_18_25.source: Derived from ONS, Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings, Table 6.1a (gross weekly pay, all employee jobs, by age group), UK 2025 provisional; ONS, Labour market status by age group (Table A05 SA), UK, Apr-Jun 2026; ONS mid-2025 population estimates
gdp_age_multiplier_18_25.derivation: For each single year of age in the band: employment rate (A05: 18-24 59.1%, 25-34 84.5%, 35-49 85.1%, 50-64 72.2%, 65+ 13.3%) x that age group's mean gross weekly pay as a share of the all-employee mean (ASHE 6.1a: 18-21 329.4, 22-29 635.4, 30-39 809.6, 40-49 880.1, 50-59 840.7, 60+ 640.3, against 757.5 for all); weighted by the England and Wales population of each year. Mean rather than median because the output-per-worker figure it scales is itself a mean (compensation of employees / employees).
gdp_age_multiplier_18_25.note: Was an assumption of 0.6. pc_start.label: Starting political capital
pc_start.rationale: Started at 60 and was raised to the top of the range, so that a full programme of actions is feasible but tight.

pc_baseline_drain.label: Monthly drain
pc_baseline_drain.description: Political capital lost every month as the crisis grinds on.

pc_delivery_per_credit.label: Soldiers per point of political credit
pc_delivery_per_credit.description: Soldiers reaching their units in a month — reservists mobilised, ex-regulars and Strategic Reserve reporting, conscripts graduating — per point of political capital earned for delivery.
pc_delivery_per_credit.rationale: One point per 500 delivered is one point per month's worth of the Army's own trained-strength gain (5,933 a year is 494 a month). The minister earns political credit at the rate at which the Army in peacetime produces soldiers, and only above it. It replaces an earlier bonus that was a share of the target and so unreachable at Corps scale.

pc_delivery_max.label: Monthly cap on delivery credit
pc_delivery_max.description: Most political capital that can be earned in one month for soldiers reaching their units.
pc_delivery_max.rationale: The same 3 as the momentum bonus it replaces, so the best possible month is no larger than before; what changes is that an ordinary delivering month can now reach it. Uncapped, the month the reserves arrive would pay for the rest of the game.

pc_refusal_per_charge.label: Refusal cases per point of political capital
pc_refusal_per_charge.description: Conscripts called up who did not report, per one political capital charged as the courts work through the backlog.
pc_refusal_per_charge.rationale: The mirror of the credit for delivery, and deliberately steeper: a soldier who arrives is a line in a statistical return, a conscript who refuses is a prosecution with a name. It replaced a flat 2 a month levied whenever willingness sat below a threshold - a switch that the Bill's age band, and nothing else in the game, reliably flipped. Cases carry over: what is not charged this month stays on the list, so no refusal is ever free and the total charged across a run is the total who refused divided by this figure. The carry-over is load-bearing rather than tidy. An address to the nation moves the refusal rate by about a tenth; rounded off month by month a tenth of a small number is nothing, and the first attempt at this charge left the address worth exactly zero in the scripted test runs - the same insensitivity as the threshold it replaced, in different clothes. The level holds the benchmark where the previous pass left it: at 1 per 200, a reserves-first programme pays 16 across a Corps run against the 12 the threshold charged it, and resigns on 35% of seeds, which is the figure unchanged. Above about 400 a restrained programme pays almost nothing and Corps falls to 5% resignations; below about 150 the programmes that conscript at scale are wiped out. Tuned over batches of 40 scripted runs.

pc_refusal_max.label: Refusal cases chargeable in a month
pc_refusal_max.description: Most political capital the refusal cases can cost in a single month, however long the backlog is.
pc_refusal_max.rationale: Court throughput, not a safety valve. However many refuse, only so many can be prosecuted in a month, so the charge is a standing drip rather than a spike - and because the remainder carries over, calling up more people makes the list run for longer instead of costing more per month. A minister who calls up several times the training estate's spare intake ends the run with a backlog the courts have not reached, which is reported and is the honest consequence: the government ends, the cases do not. The value is 1 because the step to 2 is the difference between a maximum-effort programme resigning on 28% of Corps seeds and on 90% of them, against the 20% the previous pass left it at; there is nothing between them, political capital being an integer currency. The cost of that choice: a programme that conscripts far past the training estate's capacity refuses fourteen times as many people as a restrained one and is charged the same 1 a month, so at Division it resigns on 45% of seeds where the flat threshold resigned it on 95%. It still fails the target by four fifths and still resigns on every Corps seed.

pc_idle_grace_months.label: Idle months tolerated
pc_idle_grace_months.description: Consecutive months in which the minister takes no action before the public notices.
pc_idle_grace_months.rationale: A minister may take a month to think and a second to consult. Beyond that, doing nothing visible reads as drift.

pc_idle_penalty.label: Penalty for a government seen to be doing nothing
pc_idle_penalty.description: Political capital lost each month once the minister has taken no action for longer than the tolerated run.
pc_idle_penalty.rationale: Three times the baseline drain: visible inaction costs a government more than the crisis itself does.

pc_cost_bill_emergency.label: Cost: National Service Bill, emergency

pc_cost_bill_normal.label: Cost: National Service Bill, normal
pc_cost_bill_normal.description: Political capital cost of introducing a National Service Bill under the normal timetable.

pc_cost_medical_relaxed.description: Political capital cost of a relaxed medical standard.

pc_cost_medical_wartime.label: Cost: wartime medical standard
pc_cost_medical_wartime.description: Political capital cost of a wartime medical standard.

pc_cost_exemptions_minimal.label: Cost: minimal exemptions
pc_cost_exemptions_minimal.description: Political capital cost of a minimal exemptions regime.

pc_cost_band_18_25.label: Cost: age band 18-25
pc_cost_band_18_25.description: Political capital cost of a Bill whose conscription age band is 18-25, relative to the default 18-30.
pc_cost_band_18_25.rationale: The narrowest band the Bill offers, and the one Parliament is least likely to resist: it conscripts the group that objects most loudly (18-24s, 45% strongly opposed) but the fewest people, almost none of them settled in work. Held at zero as the reference alongside the default band; the ladder above it prices the reach of the wider ones.

pc_cost_band_18_30.label: Cost: age band 18-30
pc_cost_band_18_30.description: Political capital cost of a Bill whose conscription age band is 18-30, relative to the default 18-30.
pc_cost_band_18_30.rationale: The default band, and the reference point for the other three. Zero by construction.

pc_cost_band_26_40.label: Cost: age band 26-40
pc_cost_band_26_40.description: Political capital cost of a Bill whose conscription age band is 26-40, relative to the default 18-30.
pc_cost_band_26_40.rationale: The first band whose lower bound is not 18, and the one the polling most favours: it is 6 points more willing than the default and has a quarter more people in it. What the poll cannot see is who is being taken. Every one of them is settled in work at or near peak earnings (their output per head is the highest of the four bands, 0.862), so the resistance is not the conscripts' but their employers' and their MPs'. Sized against the willingness gain it buys: crossing the willingness threshold stops a standing 2 a month, which is worth about 22 over a Division run, so 8 up front is a real price and not a prohibitive one. Tuned over batches of 40 scripted runs.

pc_cost_band_18_65.label: Cost: age band 18-65
pc_cost_band_18_65.description: Political capital cost of a Bill whose conscription age band is 18-65, relative to the default 18-30.
pc_cost_band_18_65.rationale: Legislating to conscript 38 million people, up to and including pensioners, is a far larger parliamentary undertaking than any of the other three, and it reaches every employer in the country at once. Priced above 26-40 because it is the widest reach and because, like 26-40, it clears the willingness threshold and so buys a standing monthly saving; without a price it was the strictly best band in the Bill, which is a clause that decides itself.

pc_cost_expand_capacity.label: Cost: expand training capacity
pc_cost_expand_capacity.description: Political capital cost per training-capacity purchase.

pc_cost_equipment_buy.label: Cost: emergency equipment buy

pc_address_first.label: Address the nation, first
pc_address_first.description: Political capital gained from the first address to the nation.

pc_address_second.label: Address the nation, second
pc_address_second.description: Political capital gained from the second address; nothing thereafter.

pc_address_subsequent.label: Cost: third and later address
pc_address_subsequent.description: Political capital lost each time the nation is addressed after the second, when there is nothing new to announce.
pc_address_subsequent.rationale: Mirrors the cost of blaming your predecessors again. Set below the idle penalty (3) on purpose: an address with nothing in it must cost more than saying nothing, or it becomes a free way to look busy.

raise_spending_threshold_multiplier.rationale: Game design: what 'unlocks a bigger budget' is taken to mean.

target_brigade.label: Brigade target
target_brigade.description: Effective-soldier equivalents required at Brigade difficulty.
target_brigade.rationale: A brigade group with enablers. The regulars' uncommitted slice covers under half of it.

deadline_brigade.label: Brigade deadline
deadline_brigade.description: Months to the deadline at Brigade difficulty.
deadline_brigade.rationale: Set below 12 months: with 12 months the reserves alone make a brigade several times over. Five months means the Army Reserve's 180-day notice arrives too late; the puzzle is the 90-day amendment and the ex-regular recall.

target_division.label: Division target
target_division.description: Effective-soldier equivalents required at Division difficulty.

deadline_division.label: Division deadline
deadline_division.description: Months to the deadline at Division difficulty.

target_corps.label: Corps target
target_corps.description: Effective-soldier equivalents required at Corps difficulty. The 60,000 first asked for was not reachable by any strategy; 45,000 in 24 months is the hardest setting that a near-perfect run can make.
target_corps.rationale: Set below the 60,000 first asked for: the best scripted run reached about 32,000 effective soldiers by month 15 before political capital ran out.

deadline_corps.label: Corps deadline
deadline_corps.description: Months to the deadline at Corps difficulty.
deadline_corps.rationale: Set above the 18 months first asked for: 18 months does not allow enough conscript cohorts to graduate and mature for 60,000 to be reachable by any strategy.

pc_cost_accelerate_promotion.label: Cost: accelerate promotion
pc_cost_accelerate_promotion.description: Political capital cost of running an accelerated junior-leader cadre course.
pc_cost_accelerate_promotion.rationale: Cheap, because a cadre course buys no buildings and no contracts: it is an internal personnel decision the Army can largely take for itself, where expanding the training estate (-3) cannot. It is not free, because a lever with no price is a lever with no decision. An escalating price was tried - the shape the repeated address to the nation uses - and abandoned, because political capital is abundant at Division and scarce at Corps: charging more for later courses left the Division ceiling where it was (55% to 58% of seeds meeting the target) and took an all-out Corps programme from 28% resignations to 65%. It priced the rung that did not need it and missed the one that did. What bounds this lever is the course length and the one-course-at-a-time rule, not its price.
